ASHEVILLE, North Carolina (CNN) -- In 1988, a relatively unknown rock and blues guitarist named Warren Haynes got some of his friends together to play music in Asheville, North Carolina. It was just an opportunity for local musicians to jam during the holidays, the one time of year they were all in town together. Warren Haynes' good work has been noted by the street named after him. The artists also wanted to give back to the community, so they gave the money raised by their show to various charities. The tradition has continued. Now celebrating its 20th anniversary, Haynes' Christmas Jam has evolved into an epic annual event for the musicians, fans, and particularly Habitat for Humanity. "We need Habitat For Humanity more now than ever, with the whole mortgage crisis that put us where we are now, and the fact that Habitat is about building homes for people that can't afford homes as opposed to lending money to people who can't afford homes," Haynes told CNN. Haynes and his wife, Stefani Scamardo, decided to donate 100 percent of the Christmas Jam proceeds to Habitat for Humanity years ago because they could see exactly where the money was going. They go back each year and meet the families they helped build homes for. Singer Joan Osborne echoed Haynes' thoughts. "It's a scary time. A lot of people are losing their homes so it's good to be able to do something that helps with that specific problem," she said. Going into 2008's shows, which were held December 12 and 13, the Christmas Jam had raised more than $665,000 for Asheville's Habitat For Humanity. The money has gone into building 12 houses in Enka Hills, a wooded community surrounded by mountains on a street the organization appropriately named Warren Haynes Drive. (In 2005 Habitat also built a house in the New Orleans Musicians Village.) The Thursday before the show, Haynes presented the key to a new home to single mother Suzie Cromer and her 8-year-old daughter. "Meeting the families and seeing the work that Habitat's doing with our help -- you know its hard to see that and not get emotional," Haynes said. "Warren is a hero in our mind," said Habitat's Arianne Kjellquist. "In western North Carolina, the housing costs are really out of whack with what the local wages are, so there's a big discrepancy there. There are more people that maybe would have been approved previously when the lending standards weren't so strict." This year's Christmas Jam lived up to the long-lasting and crowd-pleasing traditions of previous shows. The first night's show ran more than nine hours, ending with an Allman Brothers set after 4 a.m. The second night's show ended at 3:30 a.m. Performers included Ben Harper and Relentless 7, Travis Tritt, Michael Franti, Osborne, Ivan Neville's Dumpstaphunk, Steve Earle and Haynes' band Gov't Mule. Perhaps the most anticipated addition this year among both fans and artists was former Led Zeppelin member John Paul Jones, who played acoustic mandolin, bass and keyboards throughout the weekend with just about everyone. Jones said he was happy to pitch in. "In the economic climate like this, people really just want to get out and enjoy themselves and forget about the day to day stuff that they have to deal with. So it works on many levels," Jones said. "The fact that it is for a good cause is just a huge bonus." Haynes says the 20-year evolution of the Christmas Jam reflects his career. "We've grown up together. Its a parallel of the progress that I have achieved, and the event reflects not only the philosophy I share with these people but the mission." And as fans danced the night away while the artists played their hearts out, families' dreams of owning their perfect home come true. "I would have never imagined or dreamed that it would turn into what its turned into," Haynes reflected with a huge smile.

Christmas Jam began modestly in the late 1980s, when Haynes — already known as a formidable guitarist with deep roots in Southern rock, blues and soul — gathered musician friends for a seasonal hometown concert. The lineup has never been confined to one genre. Over the years, it has included blues players, country artists, rock bands, funk ensembles, folk singers, bluegrass pickers and surprise guests — often mixing onstage in combinations that might happen only once.

That unpredictability became part of the draw.

At Christmas Jam, the set list is only part of the story. Fans come expecting long performances, sit-ins, tributes, and the kind of loose, generous musicianship associated with late-night festival stages. The event’s reputation grew not because it followed a formula, but because it refused to.

By the time the 20th annual edition arrived, Christmas Jam had become a signature Asheville event — one that reflected the city’s artistic identity while bringing national attention to a local housing cause.

The 2008 Christmas Jam was staged as a major anniversary celebration, drawing on Haynes’ wide musical circle. As with many editions of the event, the bill brought together artists from overlapping worlds: Southern rock, jam, Americana, blues and experimental rock.

The event also continued its tradition of pairing established legends with younger or genre-crossing acts, giving the night the feel of a living map of Haynes’ influences and friendships.

That breadth is part of why Christmas Jam has endured. It is not simply a Warren Haynes concert. It is an annual convergence of musicians who treat Asheville as a temporary home base and Habitat for Humanity as the reason to show up.

The 2008 concert took place in a grim national moment.

The mortgage crisis had shaken the foundations of the American economy. Housing values were falling. Foreclosures were mounting. Banks and lenders were under scrutiny for risky loans and predatory practices. Families who had believed they were entering the stability of homeownership found themselves trapped in financial distress.

Against that backdrop, a benefit for Habitat for Humanity carried a different emotional weight.

Habitat’s model — partnering with families to build affordable homes through volunteer labor, community support and no-profit financing structures — stood in stark contrast to the speculative frenzy that helped fuel the housing collapse. Where the mortgage crisis exposed the dangers of unstable lending and unaffordable debt, Habitat emphasized long-term affordability, sweat equity and local investment.

For Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity, Christmas Jam has provided money and visibility that help turn a one-night event into lasting infrastructure: homes, neighborhoods and opportunities for families who might otherwise be priced out of secure housing.

The mountain city has long had a reputation as a haven for artists, musicians, craftspeople and independent-minded residents. Its music scene is both local and porous, welcoming touring acts while nurturing homegrown players. But unlike many destination concerts, Christmas Jam has kept its charitable purpose at the center. The event is not just staged in Asheville; it gives back to Asheville.

Benefit concerts can be fleeting by nature: a cause, a lineup, a night, a total raised. Christmas Jam has lasted because it became a tradition — and because its cause has remained tangible.

Habitat for Humanity’s work produces something visible. A family receives keys. A house goes up. A neighborhood changes. Volunteers can point to what was built. For musicians and fans, that makes the impact easier to understand: the ticket, the performance, the donation and the home are all connected.

By its 20th year, Warren Haynes’ Christmas Jam had already raised significant funds for Asheville Area Habitat for Humanity and had become one of the organization’s best-known annual supporters. The 2008 edition, arriving during one of the most severe housing crises in modern American history, reinforced the event’s deeper purpose.

It was a concert, yes — loud, collaborative, unpredictable and full of guitar fire. But it was also a reminder that music communities can do practical things. They can gather people. They can focus attention. They can raise money. And, in this case, they can help build houses.
